# The problem, the data, and how we measure {#sec-problem}

**Every result in this book is a measurement of one mapping, from a
discretized boundary and a few global conditions to the steady field that
boundary induces, on production aerodynamics data, under one frozen recipe,
with one metric.** This chapter defines the mapping on an example whose
exact solution we know, introduces the datasets and the splits that hold
out one question each, defines the metric and the instrument it is read on,
and states the protocol. A reader who knows PDEs and transformers but has
never seen this program should be able to read any later table after this
chapter and nothing else.

```{python}
#| label: setup-problem
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## The boundary-to-field problem {#sec-pde-theory}

**The object to learn is a solution operator, not a time stepper.** The
input is a closed boundary surface (in two dimensions, a closed curve) given
as a mesh of cells, each carrying its position, its outward unit normal, its
measure (area in three dimensions, length in two) and whatever data its
boundary condition prescribes, together with the problem's **global
inputs**: zero or more **global vector inputs**, directions that belong to
the problem rather than to any cell (a gravity or body-force direction, an
applied field, or, in external aerodynamics, the freestream direction
$\hat g_1$), and zero or more **global scalar inputs**, the parameters of
the PDE (a diffusivity, a Young's modulus, a Reynolds number). The output is
the steady field this data induces: pressure and wall shear on the boundary
itself, and pressure, velocity or other fields at arbitrary **interior**
points. Throughout the book *interior* means the domain the boundary
bounds; for a body in a stream, the fluid outside the body. Interior query
points carry no data; they are bare coordinates at which the field is
requested. There is no volume mesh, no initial state, and nothing to
advance in time.

@fig-problem-schematic draws the mapping on the simplest member of the
class, ideal flow around a lifting Joukowski airfoil, which has a closed-form
solution and is the running example of this book. Every dataset in the book
is an external-aerodynamics instance: one closed body, uniform far-field
data, exactly one global vector input (the freestream direction) and no
global scalar input.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-schematic
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The mapping this book studies, on the running example (ideal flow
#|   around a lifting Joukowski airfoil at 6° incidence, exact closed form).
#|   Left, the input: boundary cells with their outward normals (grey) and
#|   measures, plus the one global vector input this instance has, the unit
#|   freestream direction. Right, the output: the surface pressure
#|   coefficient along the boundary and the interior pressure field in the
#|   fluid outside the airfoil, requested at bare query points (black dots).
#|   How to read this: the figure shows what enters and what is scored; it
#|   does not show any model's prediction, and the industrial datasets are
#|   three-dimensional, turbulent and separated, where no closed form exists.
#| code-fold: true
Jk = joukowski(alpha_deg=6.0, n_cells=60)
xy, mid, nrm, cp_s, alpha = Jk["xy"], Jk["mid"], Jk["nrm"], Jk["cp_s"], Jk["alpha"]
# Interior field on a polar grid in the circle plane, mapped forward.
c = complex(-0.08, 0.08); a = abs(1.0 - c)
r = np.linspace(1.0 + 1e-3, 4.0, 90); th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 241)
R_, T_ = np.meshgrid(r, th)
zeta_g = c + a * R_ * np.exp(1j * T_); z_g = zeta_g + 1 / zeta_g
cp_g = Jk["cp_field"](z_g)

fig, (axl, axr) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.8))
for ax in (axl, axr):
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.6, 2.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.6, 1.8)
axl.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=INK, lw=1.8)
sel = slice(0, None, 3)
axl.quiver(mid[sel, 0], mid[sel, 1], nrm[sel, 0], nrm[sel, 1], color=MUTED, scale=9, width=0.004, headwidth=4)
axl.plot(mid[sel, 0], mid[sel, 1], "o", ms=3, color=INK)
axl.annotate("", xy=(-1.9 + 0.9 * np.cos(alpha), 1.3 + 0.9 * np.sin(alpha)), xytext=(-1.9, 1.3),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.8))
axl.text(-2.4, 1.55, r"global vector input: unit freestream direction $\hat g_1$", color=INK2, fontsize=9)
axl.text(0.5, -0.08, "boundary cells: position $x_i$, normal $n_i$, measure $w_i$", color=INK2, fontsize=8.5,
         ha="center", transform=axl.transAxes)
axl.set_title("input")
lim = 1.6; norm = Normalize(-lim, 1.0)
axr.pcolormesh(z_g.real, z_g.imag, np.clip(cp_g, -lim, 1.0), cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm, shading="gouraud",
               alpha=0.85, rasterized=True)
segs = np.stack([xy[:-1], xy[1:]], axis=1)
axr.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=DIVERGING(norm(np.clip(cp_s, -lim, 1))), linewidths=4.5,
                                  capstyle="round", zorder=4))
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
rq = 1.0 + 1.6 * rng.random(70) ** 0.8; tq = 2 * np.pi * rng.random(70)
zq = c + a * rq * np.exp(1j * tq); zq = zq + 1 / zq
axr.plot(zq.real, zq.imag, ".", color=INK, ms=4, zorder=5)
axr.text(0.5, -0.08, "surface field on the boundary;\ninterior field at bare query points", color=INK2,
         fontsize=8.5, ha="center", va="top", transform=axr.transAxes)
axr.set_title("output")
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm)
cb = fig.colorbar(sm, ax=axr, fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)
cb.set_label("pressure coefficient $C_p$ [–]", fontsize=9); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.text(0.49, 0.52, r"$\longmapsto$", fontsize=22, ha="center", va="center", color=INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=3.0)
plt.show()
```

**Why steady, boundary-driven problems.** The admitted class is steady,
well-posed, free of interior sources, and governed by the same equations
everywhere in the domain. For such problems the boundary data and the
global conditions determine the whole field, so a surrogate that consumes
only the boundary throws nothing away: the boundary *is* the problem. The
industrial targets are time-averaged turbulent flows around vehicles and
wings; their governing equations are not given to the model and are not
even perfectly knowable, since the turbulence closure is an empirical fit,
so every claim about an architecture is a measurement against CFD labels,
never against a closed form.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What potential theory says a correct boundary-to-field map must respect"}
For a harmonic field $u$ in a domain $\Omega$ with boundary $\Gamma$,
Green's third identity represents the interior value as a boundary integral,

$$
u(x)=\int_{\Gamma}\Bigl[G(x,y)\,\partial_{n_y}u(y)-u(y)\,\partial_{n_y}G(x,y)\Bigr]\,dS_y ,
$$ {#eq-green}

with $G$ the free-space fundamental solution, $n_y$ the outward normal at
the boundary point $y$ and $dS_y$ the boundary measure. The flows of
interest are separated and turbulent, far from harmonic, so the identity is
not a model; but it says what any correct map has to respect, and three
consequences shape the architectures compared in this book.

1. **All-to-all coupling.** The density of the representation depends on
   the whole domain, not on $x - y$ and $n_y$ alone: every boundary patch
   influences every interior point, with no cutoff radius that survives a
   change of geometry.
2. **Integrals against boundary measure.** Both terms weight each cell by
   its area, so splitting one cell into two halves leaves the operator
   unchanged. This is why every dataset hands the model cell areas alongside
   positions and normals, and why ISLA's sums are quadrature rules
   (@sec-mt2-quadrature).
3. **Exactly the shared symmetry, no more.** The map's symmetry is the
   symmetry shared by the equations, their coefficients, the boundary data
   and the nondimensional parameters. Homogeneity and constant coefficients
   buy translation invariance only; anisotropic diffusion is not isotropic,
   and the screened Laplace equation $\Delta u - \kappa^2 u = 0$ is not scale
   invariant. For incompressible Navier–Stokes at fixed Reynolds number with
   a free-space far field and the freestream as the only distinguished
   direction, the operator commutes with rigid motions, reflections and, once
   lengths are measured in a unit carried with the geometry, with positive
   scalings; the map may then depend on the geometry only through the joint
   invariants of $\{x - y,\ n_y,\ \hat g_1\}$, magnitudes and pairwise
   angles, and dimensionless scalars may modulate everything freely because
   a scalar breaks no symmetry. A ground plane, a second inlet or a Reynolds
   number that varies with size removes the corresponding symmetry, which is
   why each is a property of a dataset rather than of the equations.

Which of these an architecture enforces by construction and which it learns
from data is the subject of @sec-mt2 (ISLA) and @sec-baselines
(GeoTransolver and Transolver); none of the three requires knowing the PDE.
:::

### What varies within a dataset {#sec-parametric}

A dataset is a family of cases, and the families differ in what varies
(the datasets themselves are introduced in @sec-datasets). On DrivAerML and
SHIFT-SUV, the two car datasets, only the geometry varies: every car sits in the same
freestream, so the global vector input is a constant and the operator is
learned as a function of shape alone. On HiLiftAeroML the global vector
input is itself a variable: each wing geometry of that dataset is simulated at ten angles of
attack, so $\hat g_1$ changes from case to case and the model must represent
how the field depends on it, from attached flow through stall. Coordinates
enter only in nondimensional form, scaled by the dataset's per-case reference
length, so learned weights never see units; no architecture receives the
Reynolds number, and none is told how the field depends on the global vector
input. Because HiLiftAeroML is a full geometry-by-angle grid, its axes of
variation can each be held out separately (@sec-splits).

### What generalization means here

A learned operator is useful only if it behaves like an operator away from
its training distribution, and "away" has several independent directions.
Four are measured, one question per split, never two combined into one
score:

- **Data efficiency**: accuracy against the number of training cases on a
  fixed validation set (@sec-data-efficiency).
- **Regime extrapolation**: training on one flow regime (attached flow) and
  testing on another (post-stall), on a sealed test set evaluated once
  (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- **Unseen geometry**: validation geometries that never appear in training
  at any condition, as distinct from geometries seen at other conditions.
- **Cross-family transfer**: zero-shot evaluation on a vehicle family
  different from the training family (@sec-full-data).

## Datasets {#sec-datasets}

**Two datasets are training and evaluation sources; a third is a zero-shot
target.** All three supply the same input schema, boundary cells with
positions, outward normals and measures plus the global conditions, so one
model implementation runs on all of them.

| dataset | what it is | what varies | role in the book |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DrivAerML** (cars) | 484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants; time-averaged surface pressure and wall shear on about 8.8 million surface cells per car, plus volume fields | geometry only; one freestream | full-data accuracy, robustness probes, interior prediction |
| **HiLiftAeroML** (wings) | 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing geometries (flap and slat settings by Latin hypercube), each at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°; surface pressure, velocity and wall shear | geometry and freestream direction | data efficiency, unseen geometry, regime extrapolation |
| **SHIFT-SUV** | sport-utility bodies in two rear-end families, estate and fastback; surface pressure and wall shear; same reference length and freestream direction as DrivAerML at a lower speed | geometry; a speed shift common to every architecture | zero-shot transfer target only |

### DrivAerML {#sec-benchmarks}

Every comparison feeds the models the vehicle surface only, the information
diet of every published baseline on the dataset. The recipe assigns 435
variants to training and 48 to validation; the remaining variant is in
neither. Every experiment samples 10,000 surface cells per car per step.
The surface task predicts pressure and wall shear at those cells
(@sec-full-data); the interior task predicts pressure, velocity and
turbulent viscosity at 10,000 interior query points from the surface alone
(@sec-interior).

### SHIFT-SUV {#sec-shift-suv}

Its curated manifest separates the estate family (794 / 99 / 100 cases for
training / validation / test) from the fastback family (796 / 99 / 99). The
fastback family is held out from every model in the book and is the
zero-shot target of the cross-family transfer measurements (@sec-full-data);
the estate training split is a training source only where a two-family model
is compared. Its lower freestream speed is a covariate shift identical for
every architecture, none of which receives the Reynolds number, and it is
reported alongside the geometry-family shift rather than corrected.

### HiLiftAeroML

Because the design is a full grid, every geometry appears at every angle,
and the dataset supports splits along three independent directions: how
many cases, which angles, and which geometries. It is the dataset on which
the data-efficiency ladder is measured (@sec-data-efficiency).

### Splits {#sec-splits}

**HiLiftAeroML.** The dataset ships curated manifests, used unchanged. The
*data-efficiency* family is nested (@fig-hilift-splits): 35 training cases
$\subset$ 210 $\subset$ 510 $\subset$ 1,260, all scored on one shared
180-case validation set (180 cases on 118 geometries), with a 360-case test
set that no data-efficiency experiment touches. Because the rungs are
subsets of the same 1,260 cases, a validation geometry may appear in
training at other angles: these rungs measure sample complexity, not unseen
geometry. Two *regime-extrapolation* splits hold out flow physics: the
angle-of-attack split trains on 788 cases at angles up to 12°, validates on
112 in-regime cases and tests on 900 cases at 14° and above; the stall split
trains on 942 pre-stall cases, validates on 135 and tests on 723 post-stall
cases, stall onset determined per geometry from the lift curve. The
*geometry* family holds out 18 validation and 36 test geometries at all ten
angles, with training sets of 1,260, 210 and 40 cases (4 and 21 training
geometries at the two smaller sizes). Three *fixed-angle* splits hold the
angle at 4°, 12° or 22°, train on 126 geometries at that angle and validate
on 18 others; they remove the direction dependence entirely and so control
for whether an advantage comes from representing the freestream direction.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-splits

#|   1,800-case grid; the nested training rungs (35, 210, 510, 1,260 cases)

#|   are case counts; the bar does not show which angles or geometries fall

#| code-fold: true

shades = ["#1f5aa3", BLUE, BLUE_LIGHT, BLUE_PALE]
for n, col in zip([1260, 510, 210, 35], shades):
    ax.barh(0, n, left=0, height=0.6, color=col, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8)
ax.barh(0, 180, left=1260, height=0.6, color=BASELINE, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8)
ax.barh(0, 360, left=1440, height=0.6, color=PAPER, edgecolor=BASELINE, lw=0.8, hatch="///")
for x, label in [(35 / 2, "35"), (35 + 175 / 2, "210"), (210 + 300 / 2, "510"),
                 (510 + 750 / 2, "1,260 training cases (nested rungs)")]:
    ax.text(x, 0, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color="white" if x > 200 else INK)
ax.text(1260 + 90, 0, "val\n180", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK)

```

**DrivAerML.** One split: 435 training cars, 48 validation cars, fixed
across every experiment. Sampling-density and pose probes evaluate the same
48 cars with transformed inputs (@sec-full-data).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="The HiLiftAeroML manifests overlap, so a test split is sealed per checkpoint, not per program"}
The manifests are separate but not disjoint. The angle-of-attack and stall
test sets between them contain every one of the 180 geometries, and the
360-case data-efficiency test set shares 179 cases with them, the geometry
test set 182 and the deflection test set 182 (37 and 40 of their cases also
sit in the shared validation set). A test split is therefore *held out per
checkpoint*, since no model evaluated on it trained on it; but once the
regime-extrapolation tests were read (@sec-regime-extrapolation) no
HiLiftAeroML geometry remained unexposed at the level of the program, and no
later evaluation on these manifests is an independent program-level
confirmation (@sec-limits-validation). The dataset revision used throughout
is `bbec30bcfc6103309c1375c5228b3ad0a586bfaf`, in which six cases' force
coefficients are surface-field integrations rather than solver monitor means;
the book's force errors never use the dataset's coefficients as reference.
:::

## How we measure {#sec-part-eval}

Every number in the book is one of a small set of quantities defined here:
a relative field error, a force-coefficient error, a paired per-case
statistic, a seed-disagreement statistic, a regime-extrapolation ratio, or
an exact contract test.

### Field error, forces and paired statistics {#sec-metrics}

**The metric is the area-weighted relative L2 error of a field over the
sampled cells of one case, averaged over the validation cases, and it is
read in float32.** It scores error *per unit surface area*, so a large,
smooth cell of an open surface counts for more than the many small cells
packed into a slot or a corner. A per-point root-mean-square over the same
samples weights every cell equally and depends on where the mesher put its
cells; @tbl-metric-illustration shows the difference on the airfoil, where
one prediction error scored under two samplings of the same surface gives
the same area-weighted number and two different per-point numbers.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-metric-illustration
#| output: asis
# One synthetic prediction error, scored under two samplings of the running airfoil.
u = np.linspace(0, 1, 2001)
density = 1.0 + 14.0 * np.exp(-((u - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u - 0.0) / 0.04) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u - 1.0) / 0.04) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(density[:-1] * np.diff(u))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
Ju = joukowski(n_cells=60); Jm = joukowski(n_cells=60, frac=np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, 61), cdf, u))
def err_field(JJ):
    # a smooth error concentrated near the leading edge (where the clustered sampler puts its cells)
    s = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(JJ["w"])]); sm = (s[:-1] + s[1:]) / 2 / s[-1]
    return 0.35 * np.exp(-((sm - 0.5) / 0.08) ** 2)
def rel_l2(JJ, w):
    e = err_field(JJ); w = w / w.sum()
    return np.sqrt(np.sum(w * e**2)) / np.sqrt(np.sum(w * JJ["cp_s"] ** 2))
out = "| sampling of the same airfoil | area-weighted relative L2 (the book's metric) | per-point relative L2 |\n|---|---:|---:|\n"
for JJ, lab in ((Ju, "equal-arclength cells"), (Jm, "cells clustered at the leading edge")):
    out += f"| {lab} | {rel_l2(JJ, JJ['w']):.3f} | {rel_l2(JJ, np.ones(len(JJ['w']))):.3f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": One prediction error, a smooth bump of amplitude 0.35 in the pressure coefficient centred on the "
      "leading edge, scored against the exact Joukowski solution under two samplings of the same surface "
      "with 60 cells each. The area-weighted relative L2 agrees between the samplings to quadrature error; "
      "the per-point relative L2 rises when the mesher places more cells where the error is. "
      "How to read this: the metric measures the field, not the mesh. It is a constructed illustration, not "
      "a measurement of any model. {#tbl-metric-illustration}")
```

For one case with sampled cells $j = 1,\dots,N$, prediction $\hat f_j$,
label $f_j$ and cell measures $w_j$ normalized to sum to one, the recipe
computes

$$
\varepsilon \equiv \frac{\sqrt{\sum_j w_j\,\lVert\hat f_j-f_j\rVert^2}}
{\sqrt{\sum_j w_j\,\lVert f_j\rVert^2}},
$$ {#eq-rel-l2}

where $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ is the vector norm for vector fields (velocity,
wall shear) and the absolute value for scalars; in the interior the weights
are cell volumes. The fields enter as the training pipeline presents them,
each shifted and scaled by dataset statistics, so the denominator is the
norm of the standardized label, and absolute values are comparable only
within one dataset and one pipeline. The quantity that carries across is
the *ratio* between two models scored on the same cases. **Every
cross-architecture ratio in the book is the named baseline's error divided
by ISLA's error on the same cases, so a ratio above one favours ISLA**;
this convention is stated here once and not restated per table.

**The reporting instrument is float32 inference on the final-epoch
checkpoint.** Training runs in bfloat16 (@sec-protocol); scoring in bfloat16
adds an architecture-dependent offset of several percent to the mean error,
larger for GeoTransolver and Transolver than for ISLA, so a bfloat16
comparison would flatter ISLA. No bfloat16 number appears in the book
without being labelled as such (@sec-nb-fp32-instrument).

@fig-metric-calibration calibrates the scale of the metric on
HiLiftAeroML by scoring three parameter-free reference predictors beside
the trained architectures. It uses the gauge-pressure scale, pressure
measured relative to the freestream pressure, so the error is normalized by
the pressure variation over the surface rather than by its absolute level;
on that scale predicting the freestream pressure everywhere scores exactly
1.00 by construction, and a model has learned something about a case only
when it beats the best constant.

```{python}
#| label: fig-metric-calibration
#| fig-cap: >
#|   What a relative L2 error means, calibrated on HiLiftAeroML. Pressure
#|   relative L2 on the 180 shared validation cases on the gauge-pressure
#|   scale (pressure relative to the freestream, p − p_∞, so the error is
#|   scaled by the pressure variation over the surface, not by its absolute
#|   level; geometric mean over cases; scored in bfloat16, which predates
#|   the float32 instrument and is labelled as such; not the recipe metric), for
#|   three parameter-free reference predictors (grey) and the two released
#|   baselines trained on 35 cases, one seed, at the physical-velocity
#|   input scale. One seed suffices because this is a
#|   calibration of the metric's scale, not a comparison between
#|   architectures; the unit-direction comparison on the recipe metric is in
#|   @sec-data-efficiency. How to read this: the grey bars are the scale of
#|   the metric, 1.00 is "predict the freestream pressure everywhere" and
#|   0.93 is the best any constant per case can do. It does not show
#|   recipe-metric values, and the baseline bars measure the input scale of
#|   @sec-part-baseline, not the architectures. Data:
#|   results/hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json.
#| code-fold: true
ref = json.load(open(RES / "hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json"))
s = ref["summary"]
rows = [
    ("constant: freestream pressure", s["const_p_inf_rel_l2_gmean"], BASELINE, ""),
    ("constant: dataset mean", s["const_dataset_mean_rel_l2_gmean"], BASELINE, ""),
    ("constant: each case's own mean", s["const_case_mean_rel_l2_gmean"], BASELINE, ""),
    ("Transolver, 35 cases (physical velocity)", s["model_rel_l2_gmean"]["transolver"], AMBER, ""),
    ("GeoTransolver, 35 cases (physical velocity)", s["model_rel_l2_gmean"]["gt"], RED, ""),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.3))
y = range(len(rows))
ax.barh(list(y), [r[1] for r in rows], color=[r[2] for r in rows], height=0.62)
for i, (label, v, _, _) in enumerate(rows):
    ax.text(v + 0.012, i, f"{v:.2f}", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set_yticks(list(y), [r[0] for r in rows], fontsize=9)
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_xlim(0, 1.12)
ax.set_xlabel("pressure error, relative L2 on gauge pressure [–]\n(geometric mean over 180 cases)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The other quantities: forces, paired statistics, seed disagreement, regime ratio"}
**Force coefficients.** Inference integrates predicted pressure and wall
shear into drag and lift coefficients per case (reference area one) and
integrates the CFD labels on the *same* 10,000 sampled cells to form the
reference. The reported error is the mean absolute coefficient error over
the validation cases divided by the mean magnitude of the reference
coefficient, averaged over seeds. It is an error against the sampled-cell
label integral, not the full-surface force: the shared quadrature cancels
the sampling error common to prediction and label.

**Paired per-case statistics.** Because every architecture is scored on the
same 180 HiLiftAeroML cases (or 48 DrivAerML cars), each case yields one
paired comparison of the architectures' seed-mean errors. Three statistics
are reported: the number of cases on which ISLA has the lower seed-mean
error, with the exact two-sided sign test; the stricter count of cases on
which ISLA wins on every seed; and the median and 10th to 90th percentile
of the per-case error ratio.

**Seed disagreement.** With two independently seeded models of one
architecture, the per-case relative L2 of one seed's prediction against the
other's is the cheapest uncertainty estimate available; its Spearman rank
correlation with the per-case error against the truth measures whether the
model knows where it is wrong (@sec-data-efficiency).

**Regime-extrapolation ratio.** On the sealed angle-of-attack and stall
splits the readout is $d \equiv \varepsilon_{\text{test}} /
\varepsilon_{\text{val}}$, the out-of-regime error divided by the same
model's in-regime validation error, always reported beside the absolute
test error, since a smaller $d$ can also come from a higher in-regime floor
(@sec-regime-extrapolation).

**The gauge-pressure scale** of @fig-metric-calibration and of the
seed-disagreement analysis is $\lVert\hat p - p\rVert / \lVert p -
p_\infty\rVert$ with the geometric mean over cases. Numbers on the two
scales are not interchangeable; per-case ratios between two models coincide
on both, because the numerators are the same, and case-averaged values do
not.
:::

### Contracts are exact tests, not metrics {#sec-fidelity-columns}

**A structural property an architecture claims is asserted to roundoff in
float64 as a unit test, never averaged into a score.** A contract is a
statement such as "a rigidly moved input produces the rigidly moved
output": it either holds to roundoff on random weights and a random point
cloud or it is not claimed, so it is a property of the code rather than of
any trained checkpoint. That is what makes it worth more than a small
measured degradation: it holds for every input, including the ones no
validation set contains. What the float64 test certifies is the algebraic
construction; the residual on the trained GPU path is a separate measured
quantity, 3e-5 in float32 and several percent in bfloat16
(@sec-mt2-contracts). The contracts ISLA holds, and the tests that
verify each, are tabulated in @sec-mt2-contracts.

A property that is *not* enforced by construction, GeoTransolver's pose
behaviour for instance, is measured as an accuracy degradation under
transformed inputs and reported as a number (@sec-pose), never as a pass.

### The properties a PDE surrogate should have {#sec-four-properties}

Four properties are commonly required of any discretization of a
boundary-driven PDE. Each has a measurement here, and the measurements
differ in kind.

| property | what it means | how it is established in this book |
|---|---|---|
| spatial equivariance | a rigidly moved input gives the rigidly moved output | a float64 contract for ISLA; an accuracy under transformed inputs for GeoTransolver and Transolver, which consume raw coordinates (@sec-pose) |
| global interaction | every boundary patch can influence every output | by construction in every architecture compared: slice routing over the whole boundary, no neighbourhoods or cutoffs |
| discretization invariance | the answer does not depend on how the surface was meshed or sampled | measured as robustness to a 10:1 sampling-density bias and as convergence under refinement (@sec-consistency-bench); an acceptance criterion, below |
| units invariance | no weight sees a metre; the measure enters only as quadrature weight | coordinates nondimensionalized by every model; exact scale covariance a contract for the reference configuration and the similarity-gauge variant only; measure semantics tested by the density probe |

### Discretization invariance is an acceptance criterion, not a metric {#sec-principle}

**The goal of this program is an accurate surrogate reached by physically
principled means, because the principles are what carry a model to problems
it was not trained on; accuracy can be bought later with model size, and
generalization to novel problems cannot.** The sharpest form of that rule
concerns the discretization. The physics does not depend on how a surface
was meshed, so a model's answer must not either, in the sense of numerical
consistency: under refinement of the sampling the prediction must converge
to one field, and two samplings of the same surface must converge to the
same field, so that a different mesher differs from the training mesher
only by a discretization error that vanishes in the fine-mesh limit. Error
that falls as the sample count grows is expected, not a defect; what fails
the requirement is a dependence on the sampling distribution that does not
vanish with refinement.

A CFD mesh is refined where the engineer expected gradients, so point
density is a signal about where the flow is hard; a model that reads it is
borrowing the mesher's judgment, a non-physical input that will not be
there in a new setting. The program therefore adopts a change to the
architecture only when three questions have been answered in order: *why*
should it work, stated as a mechanism; is that mechanism physically
principled, in the sense that a CFD practitioner would accept it as a
statement about the problem rather than about the dataset; and does the
model converge to the same field under a biased and an area-proportional
resampling as the count grows. In-distribution accuracy alone never
justifies a change. Configurations that fail the third test are still
measured, as ablations that price the requirement: ISLA's routing without
its measure weights is the standing example, more accurate in distribution
on the wings, and collapsing under a sampling-density bias and under
area-proportional sampling (@sec-mechanism, @sec-consistency-bench). The
ledger of every such decision is @sec-principled-decisions.

## Protocol {#sec-protocol}

**One frozen recipe produces every cross-architecture number in the book;
a comparison that departs from it says so in the same sentence.**

| item | setting |
|---|---|
| tokens per case | 10,000 sampled surface cells per case per step, every architecture |
| epochs and schedule | 500 epochs, one case per step; the learning rate is divided by ten every 100 epochs, so the effective budget is about 300 epochs at a useful rate |
| arithmetic | bfloat16 autocast in training; float32 at evaluation (@sec-metrics) |
| augmentation | none |
| learning rate | each architecture at its declared rate, chosen by validation on the dataset's full split before any smaller-split experiment ran: ISLA $10^{-3}$; GeoTransolver $10^{-3}$; Transolver $3 \times 10^{-3}$. One stated exception: on the 35-case HiLiftAeroML rung GeoTransolver was run at both $10^{-3}$ and $3 \times 10^{-3}$ and is reported at the better, $3 \times 10^{-3}$ (@sec-fair-comparison). Above width 192, ISLA uses the width rule of @sec-using-lr |
| global vector input | the freestream as a unit direction, for every architecture (@sec-part-baseline) |
| seeds | two or more (42 and 43 unless stated), reported individually beside the mean |
| checkpoint | the final epoch; no selection on validation error |
| validation and test | all architectures at all rungs scored on the same validation cases; a sealed test split is evaluated exactly once with the checkpoint and configuration declared in writing beforehand |
| preregistration | every experiment states its prediction and its falsifier in readout units before it runs; the dated record is the notebook (@sec-notebook) |

Because the rungs of a ladder share one rate and one schedule, a difference
between rungs is a difference in data and nothing else. When a result
favours one architecture, the strongest controls for the other (a higher
learning rate, doubled epochs, a same-family architecture without the
geometry encoder) are run under the same recipe before the result is stated.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="What the validation set has been used for"}
The HiLiftAeroML and DrivAerML accuracy figures in this book are
validation-set figures with no checkpoint selection behind them, and with
this much adaptive reuse disclosed: the per-architecture learning rate was
chosen on the full split by validation; Transolver's rate was chosen per
small-data rung on it; the ablations that followed earlier readouts were
designed after reading it; and the choice of which results to present was
made with it in view. The HiLiftAeroML test splits were spent only on the
regime-extrapolation evaluations and one diagnostic run alongside them (a
variant of ISLA given raw coordinates, @sec-regime-extrapolation), and
because those test sets cover every geometry
(@sec-splits), the remaining test manifests are held out per checkpoint but
are not program-level confirmations (@sec-limits-validation).
:::

Resource matching, the statement of parameters, tokens and memory on both
sides of every comparison, is part of the protocol and is defined with the
baselines in @sec-resource-matching. Every figure and table caption ends
with the artifact in `results/` from which it is computed, and every figure
is drawn from that artifact at render time.
